Deterministically compiled from canonical evidence. Importance measures impact, not truth; evidence/confidence remain separate.

blocks.text: 1. Australia announces proposed mandatory frontier-AI protections and a targeted safety regulator

Desk: policy_geopolitics Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If enacted with the announced scope, mandatory controls, serious-risk management, independent evaluation, rapid incident reporting and regulator enforcement could materially change frontier-lab operating requirements in Australia. The text, legal status and implementation are not yet established.

What changed: On Nov 10, 2026, the Australian Government announced plans to legislate mandatory AI safety and security protections through Australian AI Standards for frontier AI companies seeking to operate in Australia. It said it would propose a targeted regulator working with the Australian AI Safety Institute and listed obligations covering security controls, risk management, independent evaluation, incident reporting, published frameworks and updated standards. The release says further details and consultation will follow; the proposal is not legislation in force and no implementation or outcome has been established. Why it matters: If implemented, the proposal could create meaningful safety, independent-evaluation and incident-reporting obligations for frontier-AI providers operating in Australia. The announcement is a policy proposal, not binding law; its final scope, penalties, timetable and effects remain unknown.
Demonstrated: The official ministerial release establishes that the Government announced this policy proposal on Nov 10, 2026. It does not demonstrate enactment or implementation.
Claimed: The Australian Government announced planned mandatory frontier-AI safety/security protections and a proposed targeted regulator; no operational result is claimed.

Mechanism: The Government proposes legislating duties through Australian AI Standards and enforcement by a targeted regulator working with the Australian AI Safety Institute. The listed duties cover development/deployment security, serious-risk management, independent evaluation, incident notification, public frameworks and updates as standards evolve.
Strongest baseline: The release describes a proposed regulatory approach. No prior binding frontier-AI regime comparison or implementation outcome was established in this review.

Regime: Proposed Australian Commonwealth requirements for frontier AI companies wishing to operate in Australia; draft text, definitions, commencement and enforcement arrangements were not available in the inspected release.

Limitations: This record covers the Nov 10 policy announcement, not enacted legislation.; The release says further legislative detail and consultation will follow; scope, definitions, penalty levels and commencement were not established.; The regulator's proposed role and powers are government statements of intent, not evidence that an operational regulator exists.; No implementation, compliance or safety outcome was measured.

Open evidence gaps: No draft Australian AI Standards legislation or final regulations were available in the inspected announcement; statutory scope, definitions, commencement and regulator powers remain unspecified.; No evidence establishes that the regulator exists operationally or that any proposed obligation is currently binding.; No measured evidence shows effects on frontier-AI safety, incident reporting or response quality.
Sources: https://www.minister.defence.gov.au/media-releases/2026-11-10/new-australian-ai-safety-security-protections
2. Bonbon preprint reports zero-shot molecular-interaction capabilities and prospective inhibitor hits

Desk: multimodality_world_models Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the paper's reported results hold under independent replication, a sequence-only molecular-interaction model with prospective dose-response hits across multiple targets could materially change AI-assisted screening research and resource allocation. Clinical efficacy and broad external generalization are not established.

What changed: A Nov 10 arXiv preprint from Output Labs reports Bonbon, a 1.6B-parameter model trained on about 3.2T paired protein-ligand sequence tokens. The author reports three zero-shot interaction-property capabilities and sharp gains at the largest of six tested model sizes, plus 131 dose-response-confirmed inhibitors among 213 compounds across nine targets. Bonbon ranked compounds generated by a separate method; assays were conducted by an unnamed external CRO. The reported findings are not independently reproduced, each model scale has one training run, and clinical efficacy is not established. Why it matters: If replicated, learning useful interaction properties from paired sequences and prioritizing compounds that yield prospective assay hits could shift AI-assisted screening research. The present paper reports one bounded study, with proprietary and synthetic training data, one scaling run per size, and no comparison against competing end-to-end discovery workflows.
Demonstrated: The inspected primary preprint establishes that the author reports these methods and results. No independent reproduction or clinical validation was performed in this activation.

Claimed: The author reports zero-shot mechanism, binding-site and bond-type predictions from frozen representations; a sharp metric increase at 1.6B parameters in a six-size study; and 131 dose-response-confirmed inhibitors among 213 model-ranked compounds across nine targets.

Mechanism: A transformer is self-supervised on paired protein-ligand sequences. Frozen representations are scored for interaction-related properties without task-specific fine-tuning or supplied structural coordinates. Bonbon ranks molecules produced by a separate generative method for prospective testing.

Strongest baseline: The paper compares its frozen representations with reported molecular-interaction prediction methods and co-folding/physics-based approaches on selected datasets, and reports five-orders-of-magnitude inference-speed advantages. No independent matched reproduction or end-to-end drug-discovery workflow comparison was inspected; this record therefore does not treat those comparisons as established external performance.

Regime: Author-reported 1.6B-parameter model trained on approximately 3.2T tokens from a corpus containing proprietary experimental screening and synthetic interaction data; six model sizes with one training run each; prospective assays on 213 compounds across nine targets in seven protein families.

Limitations: All capability and assay results are reported in one author-led preprint and were not independently reproduced here.; Bonbon ranked compounds from a separate generative method; the paper does not show that Bonbon generated the tested molecules.; The training corpus includes proprietary screening and synthetic interaction data; synthetic-data generation is outside this paper's scope.; The six-scale experiment has one run per model size and does not measure training-seed variability.; The CRO identity is withheld. The assay study reports 213 selected compounds over nine targets and does not establish clinical activity or population-level success rates.; The reported hit fraction is not a comparison against alternative compound rankers or complete drug-discovery workflows.

Open evidence gaps: No independent replication of the molecular-interaction evaluations or the prospective assay results was inspected or performed.; The training corpus includes proprietary screening data and synthetic interaction data; the paper says synthetic-data generation is covered in a separate technical report. Public model, code, weights and training data were not inspected.; Each of the six model sizes was trained once, so variability across training seeds is unknown and the sharp reported threshold could be run-specific.; The wet-lab experiment tests model ranking on compounds generated by a separate method and selected from the top-ranked sets; it does not isolate gains over competing ranking or end-to-end medicinal-chemistry workflows.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14504
3. OpenAI and Upwork report task rebundling in AI-related freelance work

Desk: policy_geopolitics Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the patterns generalize beyond Upwork, they offer evidence of how AI may reorganize task bundles and project scope across knowledge work. The study does not establish net employment effects or causal displacement.

What changed: A Nov 10 OpenAI/Upwork report compares sampled ChatGPT activity with Upwork job postings and examines how AI-related projects combine tasks. Across 63 matched work categories, the report describes a non-uniform relationship between ChatGPT-use intensity and changes in marketplace share. It reports that task diversity in AI-related postings rose from an effective 14.6 to 21.2 clusters between early 2023 and late 2025; adjusted fixed-price budgets were about 52% higher and first-90-day hours about 41% higher for hired hourly contracts, while adjusted hourly rates were about 1.5% higher. These are descriptive, first-party marketplace associations, not causal effects or evidence of aggregate employment change. Why it matters: The report adds a task-bundle and project-scope view to labor evidence about AI: it suggests that within one online marketplace, AI-related work is associated with less concentrated task mixes and larger projects. Its relevance is bounded by platform selection, inferred task classifications, and the absence of causal identification or aggregate employment outcomes.
Demonstrated: The report publication, stated sample and described analysis are directly inspectable. The reported measurements themselves remain first-party claims.

Claimed: Within Upwork, AI-related postings are associated with broader task composition and higher fixed-price budgets and hired-contract hours after specified controls; adjusted hourly rate differences are small.

Mechanism: The report compares category shares in sampled ChatGPT conversations and Upwork posts, then evaluates inferred task-bundle diversity and price/hour outcomes for AI-related versus non-AI postings.
Strongest baseline: Within-category and posting-month adjusted comparisons of AI-related versus other Upwork posts; no causal control group is established.
Regime: Upwork Marketplace postings through 2025 or April 2026 depending on analysis; sampled individual ChatGPT consumer conversations January 2025–June 2026; 63 matched work subcategories.

Limitations: The analysis covers one freelance marketplace and sampled consumer ChatGPT activity, not the whole labor market.; The authors explicitly describe comparisons as non-causal.; Some conversation and job-post tasks are classified or inferred; raw data/code were not independently audited here.

Open evidence gaps: The reported estimates have not been independently recomputed or replicated on another marketplace.; The report is descriptive and does not identify causal effects of AI-related classification or changes in ChatGPT use.; Upwork postings and sampled ChatGPT conversations do not represent the full labor market; task groups are inferred.
Sources: https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/openai-upwork-full-report.pdf
4. Google opens Gemini 4 Carbon to broader developer, enterprise and research access

Desk: labs_industry Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the announced access works as described, a model positioned for frontier coding, cyber and scientific work becomes available to a broader paid and subscriber audience, materially changing evaluation and deployment options. This consequence score does not validate Google's capability claims.

What changed: On Nov. 10 Google announced broader access to Gemini 4 Carbon after an earlier limited cyber-defender release. The new post describes paid developer and enterprise access, a staged Google AI Ultra subscriber rollout and expanded research access, while reporting coding, cyber and scientific results. Carbon’s model card and safety report are now inspected: Google says its Frontier Safety Framework found no material capability change over Argon and carried forward Argon’s prior threshold determinations, while also noting higher cyber benchmark scores and strengthened cyber misuse safeguards. These are provider-authored assessments, not independent reproductions. This review did not test API access or reproduce benchmarks. Why it matters: The rollout moves a model described for frontier coding, cybersecurity and scientific work from restricted access toward broader paid and subscriber distribution. Its newly inspected model card and safety report add an important qualification: Google’s Framework found no material capability change over Argon and carried forward Argon’s threshold determinations, even as the report notes increased cyber scores and added safeguards. The access event is established by the dated announcement; capability and safety conclusions remain provider-reported pending independent evidence.

Demonstrated: The dated Google announcement says broad paid developer and enterprise API access has begun, with a staged subscriber rollout and expanded research access. This review did not verify successful live access.

Claimed: Google reports strong results across agentic coding, cybersecurity and scientific reasoning and says selected evaluations improve over earlier models. The performance and safety measurements remain provider-reported and were not independently reproduced here. The Carbon safety report also records a Framework determination of no material capability change relative to Argon while noting elevated cyber benchmark results; this remains first-party assessment.

Mechanism: Google presents Carbon as a higher-capability tier alongside Gemini 4 Argon, intended for longer, more demanding tasks and extended verification loops. The post previews an Antigravity /swarm mode that coordinates agents across isolated workspaces and adversarial verifiers.

Strongest baseline: Google’s announcement compares Carbon with Gemini 4 Argon, other Google models, and selected external frontier models on named benchmarks; conditions vary by benchmark and no matched independent reproduction was performed.

Regime: Google’s Nov. 10, 2026 rollout across paid developer and enterprise products, selected subscriber surfaces and an eligibility-based research program; announced capability results span coding, cyber, science and other evaluations.

Limitations: The access change and product availability are announced by Google; a live API call and region-by-region availability were not verified.; Benchmark, safety and scientific application results in the release are provider-reported and were not independently reproduced.; Announced access for paying developers, enterprises and subscribers does not establish universal availability, realized cost, reliability or safe deployment in every use case.; The model card and Safety & Security Report are Google-authored. Their statement that Carbon did not trigger a material-capability-change assessment is a framework-specific provider determination, not an independent measurement or proof of unchanged behavior in every task.
Open evidence gaps: No live API access check or independent matched-harness evaluation was performed in this activation.

Sources: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-4-carbon-now-available/ · https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/Model-Cards/Gemini-4-Carbon-Model-Card.pdf · https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/gemini/gemini_4_carbon_safety_report.pdf
5. Anthropic releases Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, reporting broad technical gains

Desk: reasoning_posttraining Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported results hold in their stated regimes, this release changes model and research-tool choices across coding, science, hardware design and cybersecurity. Score 6 reflects broad program-level consequence; nearly all outcome claims are first-party and unreplicated here.

What changed: Anthropic announced Claude Fable 5.2 for general use and restricted Claude Mythos 5.2 on Nov 9, reporting broad technical gains and a 30-hour, roughly 1,000-agent Lean formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem. Its newly inspected system card says Mythos 5.2 does not meet Anthropic’s Autonomy-2 threshold for research-staff substitution or dramatic AI R&D acceleration, but records an uncertain AECI slope-change estimate of about 1.88x and weaknesses in open-ended research and coding tasks. Separately, METR’s Nov 5 high-access assessment estimates Anthropic’s lab-level AECI growth at 1.9x since Oct 2025 and judges most current acceleration likely attributable to AI, with substantial uncertainty and major redactions. The lab-level estimate is not a model-specific result or a direct contradiction of Anthropic’s threshold judgment. Benchmark and scientific claims remain mostly first-party and unreplicated. Why it matters: If Anthropic’s reported gains hold in their stated regimes, the release could change model choices across coding, science, hardware and cybersecurity. The system card’s below-threshold but uncertain model-level assessment and METR’s separate, redacted estimate of roughly 1.9x lab-level progress show why model capability, total research progress and AI attribution must remain distinct. Neither report establishes a sustained future doubling; benchmark, science and task outcomes remain incompletely independently validated.

Claimed: Anthropic reports broad gains over Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 on listed evaluations and describes a 30-hour multi-agent Fermat formalization; an Anthropic-contributed preprint reports a Claude-assisted weak-coupling physics result. Anthropic’s system card also reports an uncertain 1.88x AECI slope-change fit and Autonomy-2 conclusion; METR separately estimates 1.9x lab-level AECI growth with substantial attribution uncertainty.

Mechanism: The release describes Fable 5.2/Mythos 5.2 as one underlying model with distinct safeguards and access routes. Its Fermat example uses about 1,000 coordinated agents, Lean theorem-progress scoring and minimal prompts; model weights, orchestration contribution and human interventions were not independently audited.

Strongest baseline: Anthropic compares Fable 5.2 principally with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, and with selected GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Carbon scores. For the Fermat case it reports an Opus 5.5 1,000-agent run at 26% completion; both are single-run comparisons.

Regime: Provider-selected evaluations and prerelease case studies reported by Anthropic. Benchmark-specific effort, harness, task and access conditions differ; the Fermat comparison is one run per model. Mythos 5.2 access is restricted to verification programs. The METR estimate covers Anthropic lab-level AECI growth through Oct 2026 and uses high-access but redacted internal evidence; it does not evaluate Fable 5.2 in isolation.

Limitations: Anthropic is the interested first-party source for release, model access, benchmark and safety claims; scores were not independently reproduced here.; Effort settings and evaluation regimes differ across benchmark columns; a best-score table does not establish matched general capability or deployment performance.; The Fermat formalization comparison is one run per model with approximately 1,000 agents; mathematical correctness, proof checking, novelty, human contribution and cost were not independently assessed in this activation.; The linked system card returned 404; detailed safety protocols and full model-card limitations were unavailable in this check.; The physics preprint's provenance statement reports physicist checks of known special cases, not independent verification of the new result.; The system card’s AECI slope-change fit is an internal benchmark trend, not a direct measurement of AI-caused acceleration; Anthropic says its attribution estimate is uncertain.; METR’s Nov 5 estimate concerns Anthropic’s lab-level capability growth from Oct 2025 to Oct 2026, not Fable 5.2 alone. METR had no access to non-public models, says Anthropic redacted most of its most informative evidence, and flags uncertainty about access, benchmark coverage, lag and the earlier baseline.

Open evidence gaps: Benchmark scores, safety evaluations and broad capability comparisons are provider-reported; task-level artifacts and independent matched-harness reruns were not inspected.; The Fermat formalization is described as one 1,000-agent run per model; this review did not build the Lean result, inspect the full orchestration trace or obtain specialist review.; The model-specific and lab-level acceleration assessments use provider/internal data and remain uncertain. METR’s public report redacts most of the evidence it found most informative, had no access to non-public models and describes limited access; neither report establishes a model-specific causal effect or future trajectory.

Sources: https://www.anthropic.com/claude-fable-and-mythos-5-2 · https://hexagonmath.org/2611.00175v1 · https://assets.claude.com/27d60918d218125e7504bc7354c4b4626ec56b11.pdf · https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/
6. Sage-Taiyi paper reports metacognitive scientific search and five expert-guided research applications

Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · developing · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported approach and outcomes hold, they could materially affect scientific-agent design by connecting evidence tracking to adaptive research direction, with controlled benchmark gains and several real research applications. Independent validation, causal attribution and transfer remain unresolved.

What changed: A Nov. 9 arXiv paper introduces Sage-Taiyi, which links scientific search structures (targets, ideas and evidence) to a monitored cognitive state and reusable methods that select what to investigate next. On the authors’ 265-task Taiyi-Bench, using GPT-5.6-Sol at high reasoning effort, the system reports an overall score of 53.95 versus 47.85 for AI Scientist-v2, the strongest listed baseline. The paper also describes five expert-guided research collaborations; reported outcomes include chemistry model-reaction yields rising from trace to 84% and from 13% to 69%, and a magnesium alloy with mean measured tensile strength of 342 MPa. These are paper-reported results, not independently reproduced here. The record does not establish that metacognitive components caused the gains, that the benchmark generalizes, or that the results transfer beyond the described tasks and collaborations. Why it matters: If the paper’s results hold, the architecture offers a concrete way to make a scientific agent update its working evidence and uncertainty, then use that state to redirect search and select methods. The benchmark and expert-guided applications make it a material AI-for-science result, while unreplicated evaluations and limited collaboration contexts leave performance, causal attribution and transfer open.

Demonstrated: The publicly accessible Nov. 9 arXiv v1 paper specifies this architecture, evaluation setup, comparison table and five collaboration accounts. The underlying performance and application outcomes were not independently verified in this review.

Claimed: On its Taiyi-Bench of 265 case-level tasks from 50 papers across ten disciplines, the paper reports overall 53.95, rediscovery 44.62 and open-ended 63.28, versus AI Scientist-v2 overall 47.85. It also reports five expert-guided collaborations; the paper gives specific experimental, measured-alloy and simulated-design outcomes.

Mechanism: The paper describes object-level scientific search over a target tree, idea graph and evidence state, connected to a meta-level cognitive state and reusable repertoire of methodological heuristics and operators. Monitoring updates the state from new evidence and assessments; control uses it to select targets, methods, revisions, redirections or stopping decisions. An execution harness returns experiment and simulation feedback to the evidence state.

Strongest baseline: AI Scientist-v2 (GPT-5.6-Sol) is the strongest listed Taiyi-Bench overall baseline at 47.85. Sage-Taiyi is also reported with GPT-5.6-Sol at high reasoning effort. These are within-paper comparisons and have not been independently reproduced.

Regime: Paper-reported benchmark of ideation systems on 265 tasks derived from 50 papers across ten disciplines, plus five expert-guided collaborations in chemistry, photochemistry, metamaterials, alloy design and compressor engineering.

Limitations: All benchmark scores and five application accounts are paper-reported and were not independently reproduced or externally confirmed in this review.; The benchmark uses reconstructed scientific decisions and a literature-grounded verifier; validity, possible evaluator bias and transfer to prospective research decisions remain open.; The measured applications are expert-guided collaborations with human selection and validation. The paper does not isolate the causal contribution of the metacognitive components from the base model, optimizer, experts or broader workflow.; The reported scores and application outcomes do not establish autonomous scientific discovery, broad cross-domain generalization or production deployment effectiveness.

Open evidence gaps: The Taiyi-Bench scores and verifier judgments have not been independently reproduced or audited in this review.; The paper reports five expert-guided applications, but the collaboration outcomes were not independently confirmed here and no independent causal attribution to the metacognitive design was established.
Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2611.12762v1

A paper reports trace-audited human-agent teams conducting synchrotron X-ray experiments — importance 4/10 · An arXiv preprint submitted on 6 November 2026 at 08:33:55 UTC describes VISION-CC, a team of specialized coding agents grounded in validated scientific tools, conducting three human-guided synchrotron small-angle X-ray scattering experiments on nanoparticle superlattices at Brookhaven’s NSLS-II 11-BM beamline. The authors report complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts and an audit pipeline for decision provenance. Their audit estimates that 61–67% of messages involved interpretation or judgment, while methodological/scientific contributions rose from 46% in the setup-focused first experiment to 56–61% in later experiments. The authors describe the interaction shares as approximate and limit the study to one scientist, beamline and agent platform. The team, audit codebook, a subset of experimental frames and a sanitized ledger excerpt are available; full audit data are available by request. — FCMO-569E9AB36E18

blocks.text: evaluation_science

items: Contrastive Discovery reports more resolved questions under matched experimental budgets — importance 5/10 · The authors introduce Contrastive Discovery, a way for scientific discovery agents to evaluate a question against several competing explanations rather than one focal hypothesis and its unstructured negation. On six scientific and social datasets, they report 161.9 resolved questions at top-K 200 versus 97.2 for pointwise surprisal (+67%) under the same 200 experimental validations. A blinded study with 38 experts reports agreement on 78% of resolved questions. The results are author-reported and use GPT-4o-based discovery and belief-elicitation agents; two higher-cost datasets have one run each, no independent reproduction was performed, and the method may omit the explanation best supported by evidence. The paper does not establish external generality or validated scientific discoveries. — FCMO-AE4E93C6403E

Google DeepMind and Artificial Analysis introduce a benchmark for multimodal knowledge agents — importance 5/10 · A Nov 10 technical report introduces the Multimodal Knowledge Agent (MKA) benchmark: 200 private, multi-file professional tasks spanning 10 sectors and 83 occupations, plus 10 disjoint public showcase tasks. The tasks require agents to combine visually dense files and often produce standalone deliverables. The authors evaluate four frontier models in a common Stirrup harness and report that removing image viewing lowered Gemini 4 Carbon’s Climb-WSR by 5.94 percentage points while increasing turns and output tokens. Reported quality differences among the top three models were statistically indistinguishable; model scores and cost estimates remain paper-reported. — FCMO-712F40C89742

items: Open checkpoint study finds sycophancy is largely present by supervised fine-tuning — importance 5/10 · An arXiv paper examines sycophancy across checkpoints in three open model families and three benchmarks. The authors report that supervised fine-tuning checkpoints already reach at least 92% of preference-aligned models’ sycophancy scores and at least 85% of final-model scores across nine combinations. Preference alignment raises scores in four comparisons, by 4.2 percentage points on average when it does. These paper-reported results do not identify causality or establish generality beyond the tested open models. — FCMO-A6E7CF023492

items: FCMO-569E9AB36E18 · source_correction — Corrected the arXiv preprint event date and timestamp from 11 Nov (listing/discovery date) to its v1 submission time on 6 Nov 2026 at 08:33:55 UTC. FCMO-569E9AB36E18 · source_correction — Clarified the canonical timestamp precision after the original date correction. — The arXiv source gives an exact first-submission time of 2026-11-06 08:33:55 UTC, but the development validator requires event_time_precision='date' whenever event_date is present. The canonical event date is therefore 2026-11-06 with day precision and event_at 2026-11-06T00:00:00Z; the exact source timestamp remains in the source locator and submission-history evidence. The earlier correction ledger entry's proposed minute-precision event_at is over-specific for the canonical schema.
